div.head: Geþyncðo 2
div.ab: 7 gif ceorl geþeah, þæt he hæfde fullice fif hida agenes landes, cirican 7 kycenan, bellhus 7 burhgeat, setl 7 sundernote on cynges healle, þonne wæs he þanon forð þegenrihtes weorðe.
Et si uillanus excreuisset, ut haberet plenarie quinque hidas terrę suę proprię, ęcclesiam et coquinam, timpanarium et ianuam, sedem et sundernotam in aula regis, deinceps erat taini lege dignus.
And gif ceorl geþeah, þæt he hæfde V hida fullice agenes landes, . . . bellan 7 burhgeat, setl 7 sundornote on cynges healle, þonne wæs he þanon forð þegenrihtes wyrðe.
And gif ceorl geþeah þæt he hæfde fullice fif hida agenes landes, cirican and kycenan, bellhus and burhgeat, setl and sundernote on cynges healle, þonne wæs he þanon forð þegenrihtes weorðe.

And if a ceorl prospered, that he possessed fully five hides of land of his own, a bell and a castle-gate, a seat and special office in the king’s hall, then was he henceforth entitled to the rights of a thegn.

And if a commoner prospered so that he had fully five hides of his own property with a church and kitchen, a bell house and fortified gate, a seat and an appointed role in the king’s hall, then he was worthy of a thane’s rights ever after.

Und wenn ein Gemeinfreier [so] emporkam, dass er völlig 5 Hiden eigenen Landes hatte, Kirche und Küche, Glockenhaus (Glocke D) und Burgthor [befestigtes Domänengehöft, mehr als blosser Bauernhof im Dorfe], Sitz und besonderes Amt in des Königs Halle, dann genoss er hinfort Thegnberechtigung.

And if a ceorl prospered [so] that he fully had 5 hides of his own land, a church and a kitchen, a bell-house (bell, D) and a burh-gate [a fortified manor, more than a mere farmstead in the village], a seat and a special office in the king's hall, then he was henceforth entitled to thegn-right.
div.note: D lacks ‘cirican ⁊ kycenan’. Stevenson (with Coote) divides ‘cirican ⁊ kycenan | bellhus ⁊ b. | s. ⁊ s. | on’; the reading ‘burhgeatsetl’ (since Price–Thorpe) is ruled out by the MSS, which punctuate before ‘s’, by the Latin versions and by the rhythm. Liebermann compares Norðleod 7 ff. and Geþyncðo 3, Grið 21.1.; U: checked against Whitelock, EHD I (1979), and corrected (before: ‘And if a ceorl prospered, that he possessed fully five hides of land of his own, a bell and a castle-gate, a seat and a special office in the king's hall, then was he henceforth entitled to the rights of a thegn.’).

five hides: One hide is equivalent to the amount of land a single plowman could till in one day. During the Old English period, depending on region, one hide could equate to an area ranging from 60 to 180 acres, though it was standardized following the Conquest to roughly 120 acres. The five-hide unit seems to have been a common standard of measurement in Old English law and may have indicated the threshold above which a landowner owed military obligations to the king.
